Well, doctor, I... I suppose I’m here because things have gotten incredibly complicated at work, and my wife insisted I come speak to someone about it. You see, I work in mathematical sciences—specifically, I’ve been leading the data analysis on this massive environmental modeling contract. It’s a huge project, lots of moving parts, terabytes of data, and... well, I’ve been noticing some very disturbing patterns lately. 

I’m the lead, right? So I’m responsible for the integrity of the models. But recently, I’m pretty sure the people on that contract—the ones managing the broader scope—have been tracking my specific revisions. And not just tracking them, but actively planting errors into the datasets after I’ve finalized them. It’s subtle, you know? A misplaced decimal here, an inverted matrix there, just enough to completely skew the predictive outcomes. 

They’re doing it to make it look like I’m incompetent, like I can’t lead the work anymore. I’ve tried explaining this to my wife, and even to some of the junior analysts on my team, but they just don’t see the big picture. They keep telling me it’s just version-control mistakes, or a glitch in the repository syncing, or human error on my part. But I know my math. I’ve been doing this for decades. You don't just accidentally transpose those kinds of variables. It’s deliberate sabotage, and it’s exhausting trying to stay one step ahead of them while everyone else tells me I’m just mismanaging the Git commits.

Well, that’s the thing, doctor. It’s... it’s primarily the people managing the contract, the ones with the top-level administrative access to the data repositories. But when you ask if anyone else is involved... I mean, I don’t think my wife or the junior analysts are actually part of the sabotage, if that’s what you’re asking. No, no, they’re just... they’re just completely naive to how these systems work at a high level.

They wait, you see. They wait until I finalize a dataset, until I've checked every single variable, and then they go in behind my back and plant these incredibly specific, mathematically destructive errors in the data. And the entire point of this is to make it look like I can’t lead the work anymore, like I'm slipping, like I'm just some old man who can't handle the math. 

And the most exhausting part of it all, the thing that really keeps me up at night, is that even when I lay out the evidence... even when my wife or the junior analysts look right at the server logs, they just brush it off. They tell me it’s just version-control mistakes! They say I must have messed up a file merge, or that the system just synced incorrectly. A sync error! I’ve been working with complex computational models since before some of these kids were even born, and they want to blame it on a version-control mistake. So they aren't the ones doing the actual sabotage, no, but their blindness to what the contract managers are doing is... well, it's exactly what the people planting the errors are counting on. They know I look crazy trying to explain it.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Wrong with my mind? With my thinking? I... no. No, absolutely not. If anything, my mind is sharper, more acutely aware of the variables than it has ever been in my entire career. I mean, you don't just lose the ability to comprehend complex statistical matrices overnight, do you? My cognitive faculties are functioning perfectly, which is exactly why this whole situation is so... so profoundly insulting. 

People think because I'm sixty, maybe I'm slipping, maybe the old guy is getting confused or losing his grip on the math. But my logic is flawless, doctor! The models I build require a level of mental acuity and focus that most people simply do not possess. I track thousands of data points across multiple servers simultaneously. You can't do that if your thinking is impaired. 

So when you ask if there's something wrong with my thinking... well, it just brings me right back to the core issue here. I know I keep repeating myself, I know I probably sound like a broken record to you, but I have to make you understand the reality of what is happening to me. I’m here because I’m pretty sure—more than sure, really—that the people on that environmental modeling contract have been tracking my revisions and deliberately planting these specific errors in the datasets to make it look like I can’t lead the work anymore. They want people to think my mind is failing! They want the board to think I'm losing it! 

And the absolute worst part of it all is that their little psychological game is actually working on everyone else. Because even when I lay out the evidence, even when I show the logs, my wife or the junior analysts just pat me on the back and tell me it’s just version-control mistakes. They tell me I'm just stressed or overthinking a routine software glitch. But my thinking is crystal clear. It's the only thing I have left to rely on when everyone else is blindly accepting this... this coordinated sabotage. So no, doctor, there is absolutely nothing wrong with my mind. It's what's happening to my work that's wrong.

Well, of course there are changes, doctor. How could there not be? When you are spending every waking moment trying to untangle a web of malicious code and document a coordinated attack on your professional reputation, it... it tends to eat into your schedule. And the junior analysts I’m supposed to supervise? I’ve completely stopped being useful to them. I just don't have the time or the bandwidth to hold their hands through basic statistical regressions or review their mundane little code snippets when I'm fighting a war on the backend. I can't focus on their training when the entire foundation of the project is being undermined, so I just... I wave them off. I have to.

And then I go home, and it doesn't stop. The routine there is entirely shot, too. I used to sit down, eat dinner, maybe watch a program... normal things. Now? I mostly just keep to myself. I lock myself in the home office with my laptops, running diagnostic tools, trying to catch their unauthorized commits in real-time. My wife... bless her, she really tries, but she just doesn't understand the gravity of the situation. She’s had to constantly push me just to keep basic routines going. It's a constant stream of, "Did you eat lunch? Did you take a shower? Please come to bed, it's 3 AM." She has to remind me to do the most basic human functions because my brain is fully occupied with protecting my life's work from these people. 

So, yes, my behavior has changed. My routine is completely derailed. But it's a necessary sacrifice, doctor. If I don't sit there and monitor those logs, if I just go about my day like everything is normal... they win.

It just doesn't work like that. When a highly specific variable is altered at 3:14 AM on a Sunday, precisely three minutes after I push a secure commit to the main repository... that is not a glitch.
